newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest hydropower reservoirs near targets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest hydropower reservoirs near targets.

text.p: Hydropower reservoirs in the U.S. Northwest are on the verge of attaining seasonal minimum elevations, from which they will be allowed to re-fill in preparation for drier summer and autumn months, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said Tuesday.
"When the flood danger has passed, we will allow the projects to re-fill," said Bolyvong Tanovan at the Corps' reservoir control center in Portland, Ore.
He noted that weather patterns this year have aided flood control efforts, with cooler-than-normal temperatures helping to slow runoff from the region's near-record snowpack.
"For the next four to six weeks the water will be pounding out," said another Corps' spokesman.
Most projects have been running at "minimum operating pool," so that space would be available in case of heavy runoff, but those limits are likely to ease starting early next month.
The reservoir at Grand Coulee, the uppermost U.S. project on the Columbia River in Washington state, was at 1,212 feet on Wednesday, compared with a target of 1,208 feet.
Flows at Coulee had been held back last week in order to minimize the potential of downstream flooding, especially in the Portland area.
At that time, flows out of Bonneville Dam, the furthest downstream project on the Columbia, were being kept at 440,000 cubic feet per second (cfs).
But flows out of Bonneville are now being allowed to run as high as 500,000 cfs.
Flows out of Chief Joseph Dam, just downstream of Coulee, were averaging 220,000 cfs on Tuesday, compared with just over 200,000 cfs late last week.
Chief Joe was expected to see daily average flows of 220,000 to 230,000 cfs over the next couple of weeks, the Corps said.
